gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured heat-up time from a named tester. The one I found: Shari Galiardi froze a Renogy Core Mini 12V 100Ah DuoHeat four times, and each time it took 11–20 minutes to warm up enough to charge. Her single-pad Renogy 100Ah PRO took just over an hour.
standout_why: ChatGPT's results are maker and retailer pages: SOK, Rich Solar via Off Grid Stores, Renogy DuoHeat via Reserve Power Co, the Bely and ELB spec PDFs, Battle Born, Temgo, Power Queen, PowerUrus, Vatrer and our Redodo page. They give heater ratings and trigger temperatures, but none reports a test. The one cited source is the Power Queen page. ChatGPT took a 10 A minimum charge current from it, but I could not open it (SSL certificate error), so I compared against ChatGPT's quote of it. That quote has no heat-up time. My searches for any named reviewer's measured heat-up time on the Redodo, SOK SK12V100H, Battle Born BB10012H, Power Queen or LiTime came up empty.
decides: This supports Renogy's Core Mini DuoHeat (two pads) for buyers who need to charge soon after a freeze: one tester saw 11–20 minutes against just over an hour for a single-pad Renogy. It does not rank the Redodo, SOK or Battle Born, because I found no named measurement for them. The page can only present their heater wattage and trigger temperatures as the makers' figures.
candidates: Rich Solar 12V 100Ah LiFePO4 with internal heating

findings.label: Measured time to heat a frozen battery to charging temperature
findings.source_title: Winter Adventures Made Easy: How Self-Heating Batteries Keeps Your Power Going (Shari Galiardi, Freedom in a Can)
findings.note: Post dated 2025-11-03. The battery was left overnight in a freezer, then kept in an ice-packed cooler during the tests. The author says the time depended on how cold the cells were at the start. She gives no starting temperature for the charging runs (only 'well below freezing'). The heating source was a 20 A AC-to-DC charger or a 50 A DC-to-DC/MPPT charger, and the post says the battery needs a charging source of at least 10 A.

findings.label: Measured time to heat to charging temperature, same tester
findings.source_title: Winter Adventures Made Easy: How Self-Heating Batteries Keeps Your Power Going (Shari Galiardi, Freedom in a Can)
findings.note: The author tested this one a year before the DuoHeat and uses it for comparison: one pad against the DuoHeat's two. On her figures, the DuoHeat reached charging temperature about 3 to 5 times faster. The two tests were not run under identical conditions.

findings.label: Measured discharge while frozen
findings.value: Delivered a load of more than 14 A for several minutes with cells at 17.8°F (-7.9°C) and 28% SOC
findings.source_title: Winter Adventures Made Easy: How Self-Heating Batteries Keeps Your Power Going (Shari Galiardi, Freedom in a Can)
findings.note: Post dated 2025-11-03. The same post says the heater switches on below 41°F (5°C) and off at 50°F (10°C), and charging starts once the cells are above 32°F (0°C). These thresholds are as the author reports them, not something she measured.

findings.label: Measured heater current
findings.value: about 10 A per heating element, two elements (20 A potential draw)
findings.source_title: KiloVault HLX+ batteries, serious quality and value (Ben Stein, Panbo)
findings.note: Published 2022-05-03, from Ben Stein's teardown. At 10 A, the elements heated 'very quickly' to 'around 400 degrees' (he doesn't give the unit) before he stopped the test. He suspects that in normal use they run in short bursts. KiloVault was not among the brands ChatGPT showed. This is context for how much heater current a 100Ah battery can draw.
